---
title: "Quantum Gates — Matrices that Preserve Probability"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

What happens if we apply a Hadamard gate to a qubit initially in |0⟩?

## The core concept

A quantum gate is a linear transformation of amplitudes. For a closed-system circuit, its matrix must be unitary so the state remains normalised.

## Express it mathematically

$$
H|0\rangle=\frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** H is the Hadamard gate; |0⟩ is the input basis state; |1⟩ is the other basis state; √2 is a normalisation factor; '+' combines amplitudes, not classical stored bits.

**Substitute actual numbers:** After H, amplitudes are α=1/√2 and β=1/√2, so the two measurement probabilities are (1/√2)²=1/2 each. On 100 ideal independent repetitions, we expect about 50 zero results and 50 one results, but exact counts fluctuate.

## Why it works

The Hadamard matrix is (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]]. Its columns are orthonormal, giving H†H=I; hence it preserves total probability. Applying H again to the same qubit ideally returns |0⟩.

## Go one level deeper

A NOT gate X switches |0⟩ and |1⟩, but a general gate does not represent ordinary Boolean if/else control flow.

## Common misunderstanding

Do not treat a simulator's floating-point output as noise-free hardware evidence.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
